the first reading of Bill No. C-162, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA STEEL PLANT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Maclnnis (Cape Breton South), seconded by Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria), moves that this house do now adjourn.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA STEEL PLANT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first express my appreciation to you, to all hon. members of the house and to the government especially for the deep concern shown over this problem which has arisen practically overnight in Cape Breton.
To fully understand the impact of the announcement made on Friday by Dosco in respect of the operation of the Sydney steel plant one would necessarily have to understand the geography and make-up of that particular area of the country. The city of Sydney itself is entirely dependent on this steel operation. Sydney might be referred to as a one industry town. The announcement by Dosco, coming at this time, is a blow which that community, the surrounding communities and in fact the province of Nova Scotia cannot withstand. Such an announcement by Dosco is in effect undermining efforts made in this house recently by hon. members when the government saw fit to set up the Cape Breton Development Corporation. At that time we were dealing with a subsidiary of Dosco, and it was found necessary to take action in order to preserve the coal mines until alternative work could be provided for the men employed in that industry.
The efforts made in establishing that crown corporation were severely undermined by the announced intention of Dosco to withdraw from the steel business. I would say here and now that a blow such as this certainly undermines all the efforts that have been made in the past by members of this house and by the federal government in establishing other agencies to uplift the economy of that part of the country, and indeed the economy of the whole country. I would again refer in this connection to the Cape Breton Development Corporation. I would also refer to ARDA, the Atlantic Development Board, and at the provincial level Nova Scotia Industrial Estates Limited. All these agencies have been struggling to uplift the economy of the area in order that we may reach the level of prosperity enjoyed in other parts of Canada. A blow such as the one with which we are faced nullifies all the efforts that may be or may have been made by these agencies. Each and every member of this house has taken part in
October 16. 1967

one way or another in bringing about these agencies in order to arrive at the solutions desired by the people of Cape Breton in particular and the people of Nova Scotia in general.
With respect to Dosco, I want all hon. members to fully understand that the steel operation is separate and apart from the coal operation. I think we have dealt fairly conclusively with the problems faced by this subsidiary of Dosco. We dealt with them fairly conclusively when the Cape Breton Development Corporation was set up. During the whole of the time the economy of Cape Breton was discussed, the Sydney steel plant came in for considerable discussion.
Dosco has announced its intention of establishing a fully integrated steel mill at Con-trecoeur, Quebec. This, of course, has always been a source of concern to the people of Cape Breton. We have always been assured by Dosco that this was going to provide the lifeblood of the Sydney plant, that the Sydney plant would supply the basic steel needed and that it would survive despite all the drawbacks with which it seemed to be faced. In all probability we did not look to further developments with any great anticipation, but we were assured by Dosco time and time again that basic steel would continue to be produced at Sydney. Now Dosco has come forward with its announced intention to close the plant on April 30 next, despite the fact that as early as last spring the company saw fit to sign an agreement with the Nova Scotia government under which it would borrow $4 million and would spend $4 million over the next four years to update its equipment at Sydney.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
As a result of Dosco's decision to close the plant, cutbacks will have to be made within the next few weeks and certainly within the next month or so. This reminds me of the considerable amount of discussion which took place last summer on the drastic cutbacks in the work force at Sydney. At that time Dosco held out hopes that this was only a temporary condition, and that things would pick up. I remember reading with some delight -but now when I look back on it I am quite shocked-the announcements Dosco made every time they found it necessary to call 20 or 30 men back to work. They took advantage of this and gave it every bit of favourable publicity they could, thereby raising the hopes of the Sydney steelworkers that the situation would improve once again.
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant
I am quite sure both the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) were equally delighted at the announcements that the Sydney plant was taking back 30 steelworkers one week and 20 workers the next week and so forth, and that the work force which was laid off early in the summer was being rehired. Now they have dropped this bomb despite, as I said, the fact that they recently signed an agreement with the Nova Scotia government to spend over $4 million in the next four years. In addition the company saw fit to take part in and pay part of the cost of a recent study, the findings of which they concurred in, to enable this operation to continue.
One of the reasons Dosco gave for closing the plant is high freight rates. Let me point out that during the discussions which no doubt will follow Dosco's decision, the federal government will take a close look at the freight rate structure and will adopt any reasonable measures to alleviate the situation which has now developed. Dosco has also referred to the cost of importing European steel. I might say that this is a poor foundation on which to base its decision to close down the operation at Sydney which will affect over 100,000 people to whom Dosco is morally obligated. Yet the company considers the fact that today it can buy European steel for less is a good and sound foundation for the decision it has reached. European steel may be cheaper today, but what about tomorrow or next month? Can Dosco make such a decision based on the present price of European steel? I do not think it can, yet this is the argument the company puts forward as a reason for its decision. The present cost of European steel is not only a source of annoyance to the people of Sydney but also to the people of the United States. I have here a copy of a recent article referring to this very matter of the price of imported steel. It indicates that there is at present before the United States congress a bill to provide protection against this type of import, which is fast gaining popularity among the representatives of the United States government. For the benefit of the house I should like to read part of this article which appeared in the Financial Times:
The U.S. steel lobby has succeeded in convincing a large group of usually free trade minded senators to sponsor and support new legislation aimed at retaliation against foreign countries which discriminate against U.S. steel exports.
The bill, expected to be introduced in the Senate within the next few days, already has the support of 20 per cent of the upper house, and is given "an

October 16, 1967
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant even chance" for passage. Protectionist measures generally find this level of initial support only in the more conservative House of Representatives. The Senate traditionally backs measures aimed at promoting freer international trade.
The bill would give the president 180 days to negotiate bilateral and multilateral international agreements under which other countries would "voluntarily" restrict steel exports to the U.S. to levels no higher than their average share of the U.S. market during the 1964-1966 period. The bill, in effect, would freeze total U.S. steel imports to about 9.5 per cent of total American steel consumption.
If the U.S. failed to negotiate such "voluntary" agreements within the 180 day period, automatic, congressionally imposed quotas would freeze imports at 7 per cent of the 1964-1986 consumption level.
The bill is aimed at halting the growing inroads of imported steel in the U.S. Imports, which accounted for 4.7 per cent of U.S. steel consumption in 1961, accounted for 10.9 per cent of all steel sold in the U.S. last year, and the level had climbed to 11.5 per cent through the first eight months of 1967. Meanwhile, U.S. steel exports have dropped more than 15.4 per cent over the same period. American steel exports in 1966 came to $537 million, compared with total steel imports of $1.2 billion.
The U.S. steel industry contends that non-tariff discrimination is the basis for the domestic industry's inability to compete in foreign markets. A flat 6 per cent to 7 per cent duty is imposed on all steel imports into the U.S. The duty is levied on the wholesale value of the steel at the point of shipment and is not levied on the freight and insurance costs, which can add as much as 13 per cent to the value of the landed steel.
The article indicates the protectionist measures taken by all governments throughout the world, including West Germany, Italy and Britain, in order to protect their steel industries.
This afternoon it is not my intention to criticize the company policy which led to this announcement. It is my hope that members of this house, in the light of what they have done in the past by way of establishing different government agencies to assist the economies of different regions in this country, will see fit to apply their energies to finding a solution to this problem. When I refer to all members applying their energies to this problem, I am quite sure I am speaking fairly and honestly, because I believe all members in all parties are vitally concerned with this particular problem. Unless something is done to find a fair solution, then the efforts of members in the past in setting up these other agencies will have been wasted.
It would have been an ideal situation if these other agencies such as ARDA, the Atlantic Development Corporation, the Nova Scotia Industrial Estates and other agencies could have provided 3,000 jobs in industrial

Cape Breton. This would equal the number of jobs that Dosco say they are going to eliminate. In other words the efforts that have been made here in the past, as well as those made by the Nova Scotia government, will mean nothing whatever if the announced intention of Dosco is allowed to be carried on without definite action on the part of federal, provincial and municipal governments to offset the effects of this shocking move.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
It bears repeating that through the last number of years Dosco have consistently implied that operations at the Sydney steel plant would continue. I submit that this latest event is an indication that Dosco was not bargaining in good faith when they recently made an agreement with the Nova Scotia government and supported the recommendations of the study that was made. If such is the case, there is no doubt that this question will be given a thorough airing during the next few weeks at a follow-up meeting of the municipal, provincial and federal governments.
What I am trying to impress on the house, Mr. Speaker, is the need for a discussion of the question to be undertaken immediately. Six months is a very short time in the life of a city, and the Sydney steel plant operation is the lifeblood of the area. Within the very near future, and by that I mean during the next week or so, men in the area will begin to suffer as Dosco starts to make cut-backs. The company cannot be expected to carry on at its present level of production until April 30 next and then just cut it off completely. Steel workers in Sydney over the next few weeks, and possibly even over the next few days, will be faced with lay-off notices. Therefore it is imperative that governments at all three levels get together as quickly as possible and arrive at some decision which will avoid this drastic cut in operations.
I notice with some degree of resentment that the Hawker Siddeley group in London are not participating in any further meetings, and will not in fact make any statement about this decision; they are leaving this to their Montreal office. I cannot believe that Canadians involved in an operation like this made this decision, Mr. Speaker. These are the men who have been negotiating-we hope in good faith-over a period of years. They have been making statements about the continued life of this operation at Sydney. Therefore I cannot believe that the decision to cut off that steel operation has been made by the gentlemen in Montreal. I cannot help but think that they have been directed by
October 16, 1967

their parent body, the Hawker Siddeley people; and this group having so directed the people in Montreal, they now sit back and refuse to comment or take part in public meetings in order to fully discuss the matter. The president and the others involved at Montreal have, I think, been placed in an impossible situation here because the parent company having made this decision, they are the ones who will have to live with it. I am sure these people participated in good faith in the negotiations that have taken place, but they are now saddled with a decision which has been made elsewhere and, as I say, with which they will have to live.
I also feel sorry, Mr. Speaker, for the local management. It is not often that I stand in this house and say I feel sorry in any way for management, but I do know the local manager at the Sydney steel plant, and as late as this summer he had reason to be enthusiastic about the prospects of the Sydney steel operation. He was visited at that time by one of the directors of Hawker Siddeley in England, who was quite surprised and elated by what he found at Dosco. This director from England had no idea that they had such an establishment, and he held out great hopes for the plant. Naturally the local manager of the plant was somewhat enthusiastic about this, and he no doubt passed on this feeling to other people in the community. Now this man along with the steel workers under him are faced with this decision, which is going to mean the elimination of this industry.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, may I impress upon each and every member of the house what this closure will mean to the people of Sydney. There are 3,000 workers involved. As I have said, Sydney is a one industry town. It is also the commercial centre of Cape Breton island. Without the steel operation at Sydney the residents of the city and those in the surrounding areas will be faced with the insurmountable task of maintaining the services and upholding the economy of the community. This is a great blow to Sydney, and the only comparison I can think of would be if the seat of government were relocated elsewhere than in Ottawa. In essence, Mr. Speaker, this is what the steel plant closure means to Sydney. Perhaps hon. members can also relate this situation to the largest employer in their own home ridings deciding suddenly to pull out.
The decision to close the plant is a blow which not only affects the steel workers and their families but affects each and every man, woman and child in the area, those in the
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant surrounding towns, the island of Cape Breton and in eastern Nova Scotia. It is therefore my hope that every member of this house, as has been the case previously in regard to other agencies that have been set up, will lend his energy and co-operation to this government in trying to arrive at a solution to the problems facing the municipalities and the province of Nova Scotia, a solution which is desired by all.
May I again express my thanks to you, sir, and to the government for considering this matter an emergency, one which I am quite sure everybody at all levels will do their utmost to solve.

Mr. Speaker, in participating in this debate may I say I rise primarily because the leader of our party, who so often in the past has spoken on this question, as he did when we were discussing the legislation establishing the Cape Breton Development Corporation a few months ago, is unable to be here, weather conditions having delayed the arrival of the plane in which he was travelling to Ottawa.
I join with the hon. member who opened the debate for the official opposition in expressing the shock and dismay of, I am sure, every member in this house at the tremendous blow that has befallen the island of Cape Breton and, indeed, the whole of the province of Nova Scotia as a result of the announcement by the chairman of the Hawker Siddeley company that the steel mills at Sydney will be closed in April of next year.
This is the kind of announcement, Mr. Speaker, which in earlier years people in the South American countries were accustomed to hearing from absentee landlords, and which led to revolutions in those countries. It is the kind of announcement which people in our kind of economy have come to expect that business should have learned not to make. Nobody questions the difficult situation in which the company finds itself, Mr. Speaker, but the fact is that this company has discussed its coal operations and its steel operations with the government for months, indeed for years. As the premier of Nova Scotia said the other day, it is only a few months ago that this company received, through the Atlantic Development Board and the province of Nova Scotia, a loan of some $4 million to improve its dockage facilities so that operations at the Sydney steel mill might be more efficient and able to meet competition. The
3120	COMMONS
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant company, in following that kind of arrangement which means the virtual economic strangulation of a whole community, will have to explain its actions first to the people of Sydney and then to the people of all Canada.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Yet we should not be surprised by what has happened. Hon. members may remember that in June of this year when we were discussing the establishment of the Cape Breton Development Corporation the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in introducing the bill, said as reported on page 1553 of Hansard for June 15:
The coal problem in Cape Breton is essentially a social problem. It is because of its concern for the welfare of individuals and collectivities, and not for the welfare of companies, that the government intends to subsidize the regional economy so that it may evolve from a state of subjection to a declining natural resource toward a more wholesome economics situation.
Speaking for our party our deputy leader, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) suggested that the government had dealt with only half the problem. He said the development corporation, in addition to the responsibility for managing the Cape Breton coal industry, ought to take over management of the steel industry of that area. Our leader, in that debate, predicted that if that were not done, parliament would be dealing with another proposal for steel, similar to the one then before it, within ten years. He was a poor prophet. The period that has elapsed is not ten years; it is only four months.
In that debate we suggested that a solution to the problems of Cape Breton were to be found through a publicly owned corporation which would manage the coal and steel industries, and the resources, of the area. Now we are faced with the company's disastrous announcement.
What was the reaction of the government to our initial proposal? Reacting sharply to the proposal of the hon. member for York South the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as reported on page 1578 of Hansard for June 15, said this:
-there Is no likelihood that a take-over of the steel industry by a public corporation would command much support at the present time.
Is the minister prepared to repeat in the house today that a publicly owned corporation would command little support? Without a publicly owned corporation the problems of the area will remain without solution. Here we have a company which has demonstrated

DEBATES	October 16, 1967
that it is not prepared to take the drastic steps necessary to modernize its plant; it is not prepared to take that action which will assure the steel workers of Cape Breton that they will have jobs in the years ahead.
What is the alternative to a publicly owned corporation? Here we have a company which has made hundreds of millions of dollars in the 50-odd years that it has operated in Nova Scotia. The public of Canada has probably paid something like $200 million in the way of subventions to keep it going. Here is a company which, only a few months after announcing that it would modernize its facilities, suddenly says that in the next five or six months 3,000 people or more will be thrown out of work. If ever there was an example of corporate irresponsibility greater than that we have now witnessed, I should like to see it. In our time we have never seen that kind of cold blooded economic murder perpetrated by any company in this country.
In June, after saying that only a publicly owned corporation to embrace the steel industry of Cape Breton would provide long range solutions, we moved an amendment in which we spelled out the expanded powers required of such a development corporation. Our amendment would have empowered the corporation, should the economic welfare of the region require it, to enter fields of activity other than coal. What did the Minister of National Health and Welfare do? He argued that our amendment was wrong in principle and out of order; that the corporation would not be given the authority we suggested it ought to have, that it did not need it and did not want it.
The spokesman of the official opposition impressed me. He said that laying off more than 3,000 workers in the Sydney steel mills, apart from the immediate effect on the individual worker, will make it difficult for the city to maintain essential municipal services. But while that spokesman urged the government to give serious and sympathetic consideration to the problems of the area, I was struck by his failure to make one concrete suggestion about what ought to be done.
Our party thinks two steps ought to be taken, and they ought to be taken together. First, the steel industry of Cape Breton must be taken over by the government, I suggest by the federal and provincial governments in co-operation. The industry must be run by a publicly owned corporation. I know that some members in this house are not enthusiastic about public ownership and will only agree to
October 16, 1967

it when there is no alternative. Here, I suggest, there is no alternative. The company which is at present operating in Sydney has demonstrated over the years that it has no will to turn the industry into a viable, living, efficient operation able to meet the needs of the market and provide jobs for the steel workers of Sydney.
As I said, earlier, the first step must be to set up a publicly owned corporation. The second step-and had this suggestion been followed some years ago there might be no need for the government to take steps that some outside our group are not enthusiastic about-is to bring about a positive and rapid modernization of the steel facilities at Sydney. Without that, Mr. Speaker, this plant cannot continue. It cannot exist otherwise without large scale and permanent subsidies, which I am sure none of us would want.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The need for modernization and diversification is not something new. The government of Canada, the government of Nova Scotia and the owners of the industry have been aware of this need. Representatives of the steelworkers union have for a long time advocated modernization and diversification. In 1966 a brief prepared by Harry J. Waisglass, research director of the United Steelworkers of America, and by Father Andrew Hogan, assistant professor in the department of social sciences at St. Francis Xavier University, was presented to the Atlantic Development Board. It included extracts from a brief presented in 1951 by the president of the local union of the steel workers in Sydney, in which he said:
It is our contention that if Nova Scotia is going to develop as a part of Canada, the rated capacity of the Sydney steel plant must be greatly increased and the products diversified.
That did not take place. From 1944 to 1964 the increase in steel production at the Dosco operation was only 33 per cent compared with an increase for Canada as a whole of 170 per cent. During that period employment at the Sydney operation declined from more than
5,000	hourly rated workers to some 3,200; and not only did the number of workers decline but the wages of the Sydney workers dropped, until now they are virtually the lowest paid steel workers in Canada or the United States.
Over the past few years Canada has become a net exporter of steel, but Nova Scotia failed to participate in the production growth of other Canadian rolling mills. In contrast with expansion by the rest of the industry, the Sydney mill has been in a state
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant of virtual stagnation, and now the company has announced that it will be closed up almost completely. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that no government in Canada can permit this economic murder to go unchallenged. I do not care which government is involved; neither the Liberal federal government nor the Conservative provincial government can allow a group of company officials to write off, with the stroke of a pen, 3,000 steel workers and almost 10,000 coal miners.
A number of concrete proposals were made in the brief to which I have referred, prepared by Mr. Waisglass and Father Hogan. They suggested with respect to the Sydney plant:
At comparatively low capital cost, by making the necessary modifications and alterations to its rail mill and by the purchase of rolls, it can obtain production capacity for small and medium sized structurals in popular demand.
They also suggested:
The competitive position of the Sydney steel works on a diversified product range, including plate and rolled structurals, can be strengthened considerably by the removal of the U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel.
Some of us question some of the details, but we have had a pretty satisfactory experience as a result of the United States-Canada auto parts agreement. I can see no reason why before this, and even at this late date, the federal government could not discuss with the United States government the possibility of tariff revisions and even the wiping out of tariffs in the steel industry, something which would open up the New England markets to the Sydney steel mill. If that were done it would immediately change the competitive position of the Sydney plant. It would give it an opportunity to bid for markets in an area close at hand, rather than in the areas of central Canada where, because of shipping costs, it cannot compete with Algoma. Mr. Waisglass and Father Hogan said in support of this idea:
We recommend that the Atlantic Development Board promote collaboration between the Nova Scotia government and the dominion government in the conduct of studies on the feasibility of free trade arrangements between the U.S. and Canada in the steel industry.
They pointed out that:
Nova Scotia's steel industry has been excluded by high transportation costs from the Canadian markets in which steel consumption and production growth are concentrated, and by tariffs from its natural geographical markets.

They also suggested:
Furthermore, It is urged that the A.D.B. join with the government of Nova Scotia in requesting the Economic Council of Canada to prepare a plan for the long term growth of the Canadian primary iron and steel industry, which would indicate the nature and extent of regional participation in such growth-
All parties in this house have expressed themselves as supporting the idea of regional development. As I have said on many other occasions, I do not believe that what we want in this country is a wealthy Toronto and a wealthy Montreal with the residents of all other areas being second class citizens. I believe citizens in all parts of Canada have a right to a decent living. In concrete terms this means that an industry such as the steel industry on Cape Breton must be given the opportunity to produce, must be given the opportunity to employ its workers at decent wages.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that the government of Canada cannot permit the arrogant announcement by the owners of Dosco to go unchallenged. The government of Canada, in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia, the municipalities and the steelworkers union, must come up with a plan which will ensure the continuation of the plant on an efficient basis to meet the needs of the area and the needs of the people. This, as I say, will mean two major decisions on the part of the governments involved. The first is a decision to move immediately toward rapid modernization of the plant so it can compete efficiently with other steel producers. The second decision is that this can be done only by a publicly owned corporation.
In the light of the week end announcement by the owners of Dosco I very much want to hear from the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the main government spokesman when the legislation establishing the Cape Breton Development Corporation was being discussed. On that occasion he quickly and definitely rejected our proposal to establish a publicly owned corporation. I await with a great deal of interest his alternative to our very clear and specific proposal, which we think is the only method to solve the problem of the Sydney steel mill. The people of the country are also waiting to hear from that minister.

Mr. Speaker, the immediate events leading to today's debate are now well known. It would be wrong to say that the difficulties of the steel industry in

Cape Breton were unknown to governments, federal and provincial, but the sudden announcement by Hawker Siddeley and Dosco has come as a surprise to everybody, including Mr. Stanfield, the new leader of the Conservative party, formerly the premier of the province of Nova Scotia.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
These gentlemen-the president of Hawker Siddeley of London, the president of Hawker Siddeley of Canada and the president of Dosco-came to see a group of ministers last Thursday, not to discuss the decision but to inform them of the decision which had been reached by the company. The cabinet met the same day and dealt with this matter. There was a cabinet committee meeting on Friday and our communique of Friday night, signed by a group of ministers, suggested to the government of Nova Scotia that a meeting of people representing the local interests, the two governments, and the company, take place. At this meeting the company would have been asked to provide certain information and would have been asked to make its intentions better known with regard to the future of the plant, the future of the workers and the future of the local communities. So far as I know, representatives of the industry, ed by the government of Nova Scotia, has been refused by the company. Tomorrow night's meeting at Sydney will not include, so far as I know, representatives of the industry.
The position of the government is, first, that we deplore of course the manner in which the announcement was made, especially in view of what had been said in the house on June 27 by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury). This is found on page 2020 of Hansard for June 27. The Minister of Industry said then:
The company reports that it has been rationalizing its operations in order to improve its ability to meet increased competition from Canadian and other producers, and this also has affected the situation.
Furthermore, faced with increasing competition and declining prices in its main marketing areas the company says it has taken steps to improve the productivity of its operations at Sydney which have resulted in some curtailment of the numbers employed.
This statement certainly did not permit one to forecast a decision as sudden as that which was announced last Friday. I might also bring in as proof a report of the voluntary planning board of the province of Nova Scotia written in association with officials of the province of Nova Scotia, Dosco and the Atlantic Development Board, which was tabled in the
October 16, 1967

house, I am told, some 10 or 12 days ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). It is not an optimistic report but there are paragraphs which could lead a reader to believe there was still hope for this industry, at least in the internal Canadian market.

Second, the government intends to hold the company responsible not only for its legal obligations, which of course the company accepts-and the legal obligation is limited-but also for some moral responsibility to the labour force and the communities of Sydney and the surrounding area. It is too easy for a company to live in and on a community and then say with only a day or two days' notice, "We are leaving. Catch." I believe that a company like this has some responsibility. We intend to remind the company of that fact.
In respect of the problem itself we intend to find out what are the facts which led to this decision. We also intend to take all reasonable steps to help individuals, of course, and the province which has the main responsibility in this matter. In so saying I am not trying to pass the buck. I am just stating the fact that this is a problem of one industry; it is not a problem involving the whole Canadian industry. In the last few days, as a matter of fact, and rightly so, the provincial authorities have indicated clearly that they are considering the problem in this way. As I have said, the meeting tomorrow night has been called by the government of Nova Scotia. We intend to be present and take part in a most constructive fashion.
Finally, it is too early to say what will be done by the central government to help in this very serious matter. I think it would be unwise, before the meetings to which I have referred take place, to state our plans. I should like to say only that we will be and are exploring all rational avenues in an effort to help.
The speaker who preceded me, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow),

It would be necessary to know first whether nationalization would solve the problem and what nationalization of that one plant would lead us to. If we were to automatically nationalize mines which have exhausted their ore or if we were to get into the habit of nationalizing individual plants which get into great difficulties, the government would have a full time job on its hands. There are plants such as textile plants in the ridings of many hon. members, there are also gold mines in northern Quebec and northern Ontario, which probably would be asking the next day for a similar advantage if nationalization can be considered so automatically to be an advantage.
The problems of Cape Breton are deep ones. The economic base itself of Cape Breton has been eroding away for a good number of years. This means essentially the coal and steel industries. The job now is to find an alternative economic base. Everyone will agree that this is not an easy task, but my belief is that it is not an impossible one.
I should like to use the next few minutes to give a report on some constructive moves taking place in Cape Breton now, mainly pertaining to the Cape Breton Development Corporation for which I am responsible to parliament.

You will recall Mr. Speaker, that a few days ago, the Prime Minister announced the appointment of Mr. Robinson Ord, vice president of Chemcell, to head the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The appointment of Mr. Ord was greeted with great satisfaction by the provincial government, by the labour unions in the area, by the local and national press. I have no intention of reading all the reports to you. But, generally speaking, they are most favourable. For instance, the Chronicle-Herald on September 16 wrote:

The article in the Chronicle-Herald of September 16, 1967 says in respect of Mr. Ord:
His acceptance of the position indicates an admirable courage, for no one doubts that it will be difficult and often frustrating-
Mr. Ord's background in the chemical industry is in line with some of the hopes of the planners, who see a considerable development of that industry in Cape Breton. More, his experience in other places, and in endeavours largely unfamiliar here, should bring a new and helpful perspective to the campaign to diversify the island's economy.

Perhaps I should say a little more about this subject. I think everyone will agree that there are in Cape Breton two main areas for future potential development, the Point Edward industrial park near Sydney and the Strait of Canso area. Having regard to the first, I want to emphasize what the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Mac-Innis) said about the tremendous amount of work which is being done in this area at this time. I have an up to date report from the Atlantic Development Board on that matter.
The number of studies which have been made is considerable, and while I agree that studies do not solve problems they have a tendency to help in finding solutions. Studies have been made of industrial park needs, of industrial opportunities, and of the layout and design for the Point Edward industrial park. There have also been studies of local government in industrial Cape Breton, of the availability of fresh water for fish plants, of the Cape Breton Island tourist industry, of fisheries resources and of industrial feasibility in several small industries.
From this limited list I think one must realize that the background of information on Cape Breton is getting better. It is my belief that everyone will benefit from the increased background information but specially the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
On the subject of realizations, may I say that people may not at this time have complete enough information on what is taking place in that area. I have a list of the various things which have been accomplished. In respect of basic services for the Point Edward industrial park a bulk handling facility, representing a cost of $950,000 is to be completed early in 1968. There is also a water-for-existing-industries-project, an expenditure of 270,000, which was completed in April of this
October 16, 1967

year. There is a recirculation of water project for the Pyromineral company at a cost of $150,000 to be completed next year. There is a sewage treatment plant at a cost of $400,000 to be completed next year. Dredging of the port has been completed at a cost of $162,000. A temporary wharf at a cost of $70,000 was completed last year as well as additional services for the park at a cost of $1,400,000. One could go on listing these things which have been done or are in progress to improve the facilities of the Point Edward industrial park.
I could also list a number of things done by other federal departments, particularly by the area development agency of the Department of Industry. Out of the 101 projects in Nova Scotia now approved eight are in Cape Breton. They have an estimated expenditure of $134 million, which represents either directly or indirectly 1,200 jobs. Out of 11 new projects coming up for approval five are for Cape Breton and represent a capital expenditure of $70 million, $10 million of which will come from ADA. This will mean 2,000 more jobs either directly or indirectly. One can readily see that what has been done in Cape Breton, at Point Edward in particular, represents an important step in the right direction.
I could also point out the industrial development taking place there and the federal contribution to that development. I could talk, for example, about the heavy water plants at Glace Bay and at Port Hawkesbury made possible by Atomic Energy of Canada's purchases.
Perhaps I should mention the fact that the FRED program in Nova Scotia is coming along nicely. Everyone realizes that the local problem is wider than even Cape Breton itself. Hon. members know that the FRED program under ARDA will bring in not only the four counties of Cape Breton Island but also the five mainland counties of Cumberland, Antigonish, Pictou, Guysborough and Colchester.
At the moment the government of Nova Scotia is establishing an organization within the cabinet of that province which will make effective provincial participation possible. The provincial response to the request for the appointment of a senior cabinet committee headed by the premier himself has been satisfactory.
Let me say a final word or two about the Strait of Canso area. I was there recently and was impressed by the quality of the location for industrial development and also by the facilities offered by that port for these great new ships of the future in the 200,000 ton to

Those of you who have been there recently know that there is already on location a gypsum shipping operation, a pulp and paper plant and a tank farm for the operations of the British American Oil Company. Canadian General Electric is constructing a heavy water plant and there is also at this time a thermal power station being built. C.I.L. is planning a chemical plant and Nova Scotia Pulp Limited proposes to expand its present establishment. British American Oil also has a big new project to establish a refinery in the area which will be the cornerstone of what everyone hopes will become an important petrochemical complex. This project is presently the object of a three-corner negotiation involving B.A., the Nova Scotia government, the federal government and the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
I understand as well as everyone the potential and tragic results to the area of the announcement last Friday. I sympathize, as everybody does, with the situation in which these steel workers are being placed. For my part, and on behalf of the government, I can only say that we will approach this problem with the fullest co-operation with the people involved and the provincial government of Nova Scotia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the motion for adjournment made by the hon. member for Capre Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) as well as to his reasons therefore.
As a matter of fact, this motion for adjournment is made as a result of economic conditions which do not look promising for Nova Scotia and especially for the Cape Breton area. It is once again an economic situation which calls for this adjournment.
We could have made a motion for adjournment about the gold mines in north-western Quebec which are in the same situation. We could have made a motion for adjournment to assist agriculture because it is in a bad way in many areas of Canada. We could have done the same thing in connection with other areas, even though the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) tells us that it is not the general economy which is in a sad plight, but only one sector of it.
If to the steel industry one adds the gold mines, agriculture, and the uranium mines, areas which were all in a deplorable state not so long ago, one must conclude that our economy is very sick indeed. And the reason for that is very simple, it is because we are not masters of our economy. Our economy is under foreign control and we are at the mercy of foreigners.
Dosco, in Cape Breton, wants to sell its primary production and the only buyer, it seems, is our neighbour to the south who sets the price. It does not buy at the price set by Dosco, it sets the price for Dosco, Dosco pays salaries and operation costs and as it operates at a loss, of course, the government must subsidize it. And the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) said a little earlier that the federal government had undoubtedly paid over $200 million in subsidies. The hon. member for Winnipeg North seemed to insinuate that those $200 million had been paid to the company to enable it to make a profit. But the opposite is happening. Being short of subsidies, the company can not maintain its operations. It will have to close down next April, and throw out about 3,000 workers.
Mr. Speaker, as long as we will not manage our own affairs and will not decide, here in Canada, to demand prices based on the cost price, we will not get rid of subsidies. The government grants subsidies to gold mining exactly for the same reason, that is because the United States, and not the Canadian government fix the price at $35 per ounce. Our Canadian government is like a puppet controlled by the United States. Up until now, this has been the only role played by the Canadian government.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is impossible to make a decision. We ask the minister: Does the government intend to raise the price of gold? No, the United States object to that. The situation is the same with regard to steel. It is impossible to obtain the price needed for normal operations. Therefore the plant closes down and Canadians lose their jobs. This situation exists in many sectors.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) suggests nationalization, that the government buy Dosco or other companies operating in Cape Breton, modernize the plants and improve production. But modernisation and automation, Mr. Speaker, will likewise produce lay-offs. And if we increase the production of these mines, steel plants or iron works, if we sell to the United States at a loss, we will still have to grant subsidies. We will still be struggling with, on the one hand, subsidies covered by the taxes paid by the people and, on the other hand, the transfer of manpower.
Just imagine how much work will befall upon the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) in Canada, what with all those problems: to relocate Cape Breton people to Mattagami, north of Amos, or to Thompson, in northern Manitoba. We do not know where to send these people anymore, because of the lack of new secondary industries. This problem does not arise only in Nova Scotia. We heard talk, especially this past week-end, about the need for secondary industries in the province of Quebec. There are even some who envoked the need of a special status in order to secure secondary industries.
We have the same problems as Nova Scotia. This is an economic problem, which is common to all provinces.
And why is Sidbec, another steel company, but in Quebec this time, not in operation? Why? Because of a lack of technicians, of engineers, of goodwill, of human capital No.

Ociober 16, 1967	COMMONS
Because of a lack of opportunities. No. Because American interests have decided that Sidbec will not start its operations. And Sidbec is waiting. Millions were invested in it, but it remains idle, in spite of the fact that the provincial government is directly involved as well as individuals. Everybody wants to see the development of a primary steel processing industry which would put out the primary production which, at present, is wholly sold to the United States.
Whose secondary industries process our steel and send it back to us after making a profit, at our expense, naturally. That is the situation, and nothing else.
And what if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources were to tell us that a paper mill or an industrial park is being built or that another tourist organization is being developed, which the Cape Breton Development Corporation can help by every possible means? Yes, but how, by what means? By means of subsidies? And that, to promote primary production, everything else being left under the control of Americans. That is the problem, Mr. Speaker. I have nothing against Americans, but it seems to me that the government should argue with them and tell them: Listen, we are quite willing to let you have raw materials, primary products, but let us at least partly process those goods. When it is a question of manufacturing freezers, cars, of finishing a product made of steel, everything is controlled, everything is made in the United States. Nothing is made in Canada.
When we have an opportunity to develop or to continue developing our production, it seems that at that moment the government withdraws and forgets its responsibilities. It does no more than agree to an emergency debate which will not solve the problem of Cape Breton. Note that there is no legislation, there is nothing before the house.
We are discussing a situation in fact. Something that exists. Dosco will close its doors in April just as in our own area, gold mines will close their doors and have been closing them for a few years with the result that manpower must be transferred, moved here and there and, meanwhile, the economy of Canada is going to pot. Why? Because no solution is being suggested. The solution of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) is nationalization. What would it bring? Absolutely nothing. We have seen plenty of government ownership and nationalization.

Mr. Speaker, a few months ago when we were debating the bill to set up the Cape Breton Development Corporation, I am sure most members of the house felt this matter would not be back with us so soon. One must regret the announcement made by the Hawker Siddeley Company which can be used, as it has been used so devastatingly, against private enterprise. One would expect such action possibly from a British based company, knowing the economic or uneconomic basis of a socialized steel industry and
October 16, 1967	COMMONS
having had the experience of seeing the steel industry of that country nationalized, denationalized and nationalized again. It is not surprising either that this solution should come readily to the minds of some members of this chamber.
We know also that the steel industry is one of those industries like the aircraft industry in that it is a status symbol for the developing nations of the world. We know that a tremendous amount of the steel production in foreign countries has nothing whatever to do with economics but has everything to do with local feelings of nationalism and with assistance from the developed countries around the world. It is quite possible that through some of our aid programs we have been the authors of the distress the Canadian steel industry now faces.
The success of the Cape Breton Development Corporation requires the closest cooperation between private industry and government. I am afraid that this has not been accomplished in the months since the legislation was passed. Certainly we hope that provincial negotiations will come about and that the federal government will lend all the assistance it can. Co-operation with private industry must not be ruled out. It is, I suppose, a commentary on the way steel industries around the world have fallen victim to nationalization that any possibility of interesting private capital in the steel industry of this nation is remote. It would be worth the government's time, however, to pursue the question of the participation of private enterprise in the maritime and Canadian economies because it will be a sadder day still if all industrial decisions in this country cease to be based on economics and become entirely political.

People in governmental circles have been greatly fooled by this corporation, and in saying that I do not reflect on the members of any government involved. We in Canada, I think, are used to taking people at their word. In this instance their words were not worth anything.
In the Cape Breton Post for May 27 last the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) was quoted, in reference to the $4 million granted by the Atlantic Development Board and the province of Nova Scotia to improve dock handling facilities at Dosco, as saying:
"The new and improved facilities should significantly reduce handling costs and improve the competitive position of the Sydney steel industry," he said.
"And with this government assistance, it is expected that additional company capital will be freed to completely modernize the Sydney steel plant itself and bring its operating costs closer to those of other Canadian steel companies."
Mr. MacEachen said that in terms of employment he is "extremely optimistic" that these developments will be beneficial over the long term.
I have no doubt that the Minister of National Health and Welfare made that statement in good faith. But he, along with so many of us, is misinformed and misled by this corporation. Just a few years ago, in 1962, members of parliament of all parties

and senators of all parties were invited to the Chateau Laurier by Mr. T. J. Emmert, the man who made this shocking announcement a few days ago. He wanted to get to know the members of the government and members of parliament. He had glowing words for what was going to take place in the future under Hawker Siddeley. Perhaps we are all from Missouri, Mr. Speaker, but we found this difficult to believe.
In any event, following this introduction he wrote me a letter which I should like to place on record. I assume that all members of this house and senators received a similar letter. It is dated March 16, 1962 and reads:

I could refer to other glowing statements, references to making Sydney the Pittsburgh of Canada and that they were going to do this and do that. Someone or other was always making some sort of statement. Then the other day this gentleman took off for Britain in a great hurry, I understand, not even having time to meet with either the federal or provincial cabinets.
I think it is time that governments in Canada, regardless of political stripe and be they provincial or federal, inform these people without hesitation and in no uncertain terms just how they feel. During the period when there have been problems in respect of steel, which goes back quite a few months, we on this side of the house have questioned the Prime Minister, the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) with regard to exports. In less than six months, if they have their way, the Sydney steel plant will go out of existence. In ten years, since Hawker Siddeley bought the steel plant for a song, this company has wrought the destruction of the only basic steel industry in eastern Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that those who have already taken part in the debate have given a pretty clear idea of the scope of the problem we are discussing this afternoon.
Of course, the situation in Sydney is quite unusual, in that it involves the sudden collapse of the entire economy of a city, of a community. As the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) said earlier, without some government intervention, one fails to see how the people can remain hopeful.
Now, Mr. Speaker, even though the case of Sydney presents some particular tragic aspects, the fact remains that such situations are becoming more frequent in Canada. At present, Sydney is involved; at one time, it was Bell Island in Newfoundland. Other such cases occurred in Manitoba and every day, we learn that large establishments are closing down, undergoing some changes, being transferred or disappearing. It seems that the very essence of our modern economy tends to bring about tremendous changes.
For Sydney, it is probably more tragic as it was for Bell Island. In the case of Bell Island, there was only one industry from which the whole community drew its income and, at a moment's notice, we learned that the business was shutting down, that the people were out of work and that the only source of income for the community had dried up.
Obviously, I do not think that anybody in this house can find a magic solution to any problems which might occur in this field. But what strikes me especially, in the case of Sydney, is the fact that the officials of the company behave as if thousands of people were not really involved and that after concluding what they call their profitable operations, all they had to do was simply to close down the place and say: "Goodbye, gentlemen, we are not making money any more in Sydney. It is not an economic operation."
We know fully well that there is not one single business in Canada which does not benefit, in its establishment, in its operations,
October 16, 1967

Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant from the human contribution of the workers, first, of the cities and towns where it is established, in short, which does not benefit from the social and economic sub-structure of our society. Such is the case for Sydney; the company took advantage of all those benefits and now all we get is a few months' notice.
We are quite aware that cities such as Montreal and Toronto may easily absorb, relatively speaking, 300, 400 or even a few thousand people, but we also know that, in the case of Sydney, this is not possible. When the steel-works are closed down, this community will be faced with an insoluble problem, and we shall also be faced with an extremely difficult problem.
There will be dismissals, lay-offs brought about by technological changes, or simply by an industry closing down. I cannot get it into my head that a company which knows, not just a month or two, but often several years in advance, that it will have to close down or to alter its operations, thus seriously affecting a great many people, should consider that its responsibilities are over just by giving notice of its intentions a few months in advance.
Since this sort of thing happens more and more often, Mr. Speaker, I wonder-I am merely asking myself a question, but very seriously-whether, since it seems that some companies are not willing to consider this human aspect of their activities, we should not force them to do so through legislation. Otherwise, we will be faced with this sort of problem every day, people will be affected because they were only given a few months' notice. At present there is the case of Sydney, but there may be others. At any given moment, a company may start a business in the far North, for example, get families to move there because it needs them, and then one day decide that this particular undertaking is no longer economic and say to its employees: beginning today, we are pulling out; you are on your own.
Therefore, I think it would be childish for the House of Commons to believe that we can prevent such things from happening or such closings. They are unavoidable; and will likely become more and more so.
But I think that we should anticipate, either by legislation or otherwise, in what conditions this should come about, so that human beings are not made the victims of decisions taken behind closed doors by a company's board of directors.

Mr. Speaker, in a short period of time I just wish to endorse the suggestions and submissions made by my colleagues, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir), on this very important matter. I listened very intently to what the two members on the treasury benches who spoke had to say. I made notes on the remarks of all the speakers who preceded me. I believe that some of the suggestions and submissions they made are most interesting and should be taken into account at this time.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the Sydney steel plant is the only basic steel plant in the Atlantic area. It is important not only to the Sydney area but to other areas of the province of Nova Scotia and undoubtedly to other areas in the Atlantic provinces. As the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria suggested, there are in my constituency the Trenton plants which are owned by the company that owns the Sydney steel plant. There are several industries operated by the
October 16, 1967

Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant Hawker Siddeley group, including the Eastern car company, the Trenton steel works and Trenton Industries Limited.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I suggest that the company which would be most affected by the proposed closure would be the Trenton steel works where axles are made for railway cars. This is the only company in Canada which makes axles, and the ingots and billets are taken from Sydney to the Trenton steel works. There one of the largest hammers in Canada and indeed in North America pounds these ingots and billets which are then sent on for finishing. The closure would be important to many employees in my area working in the axle-hammer department and the axle-finishing department, and in the marine forging and marine finishing departments which carry out heavy forging of products such as propellor shafts for ships in this country. Undoubtedly the people in my constituency as well as the people of the Cape Breton area and indeed in the whole of the Atlantic region are most apprehensive about this proposed closure.
The hon. members for Cape Breton South and Cape Breton North and Victoria have always been in the forefront in bringing forward suggestions of importance to their area. They have been most vociferous, and properly so, in speaking for their constituents ever since they came to the house. It has indeed been a pleasure to be associated with these two members who have done so much for their constituencies. It was suggested by these gentlemen that since Hawker Siddeley is a British Company it should take some responsibility for the proposed policy of Dosco. I think the Globe and Mail of this morning contained a very good article with reference to this matter. When the present chairman of the Hawker Siddeley group, Sir Harold Hall, came to Canada in the last few days he was asked whether as head of the Dosco parent company he could explain why the steel operation was being closed. He said:
This is happening in Canada, not England. I am afraid I must refer you again to Montreal.
I suggest that if a company, regardless of where it comes from, buys a Canadian company and establishes a policy of employment, or in this case a policy of unemployment, then it must be ready to stand behind such a policy and be responsible to the Canadian government and to the people in the areas where the industry is located. The senior Canadian officials of the company obviously had to abide by what was dictated by the

directors of the parent company. If such was the case, then let the officials of the parent company come here and speak out and bear the responsibility for what they have done. Let them come to a meeting. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) as well as the officials of the government of Nova Scotia would be very happy to meet the officials of the company, not only those in Canada but those of the Hawker Siddeley group in England, and I hope this will be done.
As has been said, Cape Bretoners and people generally in the Atlantic area have been apprehensive about what would happen under Hawker Siddeley. I remember that in 1957 there was much apprehension both in my area and in Cape Breton. I remember that municipal officials met with many people in Sydney as well as in my area and repeated what the company had said before the board of trade in Sydney as to what they could do for the area. I am afraid this is not what happened. The article in the Globe and Mail contains the following statement:
Cape Bretoners have feared mill abandonment for decades, particularly in recent years as they have watched Dosco close mine after mine in Cape Breton, pull out of coal mining in Cumberland county on the Nova Scotia mainland, and abandon all but one mine in Pictou county. It closed its limestone quarrying operations and iron ore mining in Newfoundland while opening a new steel fabricating plant in Quebec. The Hawker Siddeley group took control of Dosco in 1957.
What I cannot understand, along with the former and present premiers of Nova Scotia as well as many other people including the federal authorities, is the reason for this rapid change. It has been said many times by Dosco that the Quebec mill at Contrecoeur would be a boost for Sydney and would provide a new market for basic steel. The present premier of Nova Scotia has stated that this proposed closure is an incredible change of attitude.
I listened with interest to what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) has to say, particularly with regard to the joint report of the voluntary economic planning board of Nova Scotia, the Atlantic Development Board and Dosco as well as some federal officials. I have not read the report but I would like to. The minister said that some parts of the report lead one to believe that the industry still has a chance This is what I cannot understand. It seems very strange that immediately after this report was tabled this company should have come to the federal officials and to the Nova

Scotia government and said "We are closing this plant". I know that as soon as this report was made the voluntary economic planning board of Nova Scotia set up a committee headed by Rev. J. H. MacNeil of the extension department of St. Francis Xavier university to study the report fully. I think there is still time for it to be studied.

I was interested in the suggestions put forward by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand).
