speakeroldname: Mr. J. B. Siewari (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA STEEL PLANT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
there is no doubt whatever in my mind, after listening to those who have spoken already, that the House of Commons will want the government of Canada to be as helpful as possible and proper to the government of Nova Scotia and to all others immediately challenged by the decision announced by Dosco last Friday. In any examination of what will have to be done in these circumstances, the point of departure must be the report issued in September, 1967, as the result of a study of the Sydney steel industry by the voluntary economic planning board of the government of Nova Scotia. I should like, therefore, to put before hon. members the basic observations in that report.
Evidently the question raised was Whether or not diversification of the steel-making operations at Sydney would be warranted. In no place in the report is it stated that this is the question on which the focus is concentrated, but I think if one reads the report carefully it will be clear that this was the topic to which those making the study were directing their attention chiefly. The answer to that question was in the negative.
However, the report is based on the assumption that the present operations at Sydney are economically sound, and it was made as late as September, 1967. It was prepared with the co-operation of high officials of Dosco who made available information which, because it concerns the company's competitive position, was not made public. In other words, this is a report prepared with the co-operation of Dosco and issued with the approval of Dosco. On pages 21 and 22 of the report we find the very question that is before this house this afternoon. I quote:
What, then, are the future prospects for steel making at Sydney? The mill has a continuing but

irregular demand for rails, which cannot be expected to increase but which may continue to provide a useful source of sales. In addition the Atlantic provinces provide a small but growing source of demand for such rolled products as concrete reinforcing bars and small structurals which Sydney can provide. Thirdly, there is an existing captive demand for billets and ingots from Dosco's mills in Quebec. While a general slackness in business has recently reduced this demand, it should revive with improved business conditions and expand considerably as the flat rolling mills are brought fully into commercial operation. Sydney can be expected to continue to supple ingots and billets to Contrecoeur for many years provided it is economic to do so. More specifically it will continue at long as the current production costs plus freight are less than the variable and fixed costs including capital charges of new steel-making facilities at Contrecoeur.
It is quite clear that the basic assumption is that the basic operations at Sydney are at the moment economically viable. Despite that assumption, I think we have to recognize that the analysis of steel making at Sydney was sombre and depressing.
What the report states in this connection is that whereas 50 years ago the proximity of a steel mill to coal and iron ore was the basic consideration in determining whether or not a mill in a particular location was economically sound, this is no longer the case. The reason for this is that new technology has reduced the amount of coal that is necessary to produce a ton of finished steel, and the discovery of high-grade ores along with techniques for refining low-grade ores has made it economically possible to bring the ores to mills situated far away from the source of these ores. Moreover, the importance of scrap in the steel-making process has tended to act as a magnet to draw steel production toward centres of population.
Of course, when you take into consideration two additional factors I think you see how serious was the problem that concerned the voluntary economic planning board. One is that the coal in the Cape Breton mines came to be of increasingly little value for steel processing because of its high sulphur content. Then the discovery of iron ore bodies elsewhere tended to make reliance on Wabana unnecessary and, indeed, put Bell Island out of business. The report says that the logical location for steel production today is not where the raw materials are but close to markets.
Now, unfortunately, markets in the Atlantic region are small. The report says that in 1966 Nova Scotia had about 10.2 per cent of Canada's steel production capacity but that the steel products made at Sydney and consumed in the Atlantic region amounted to
October 16. 1967

only about 1.8 per cent of Canadian production. The report points out also that today the most successful steel-making operations are those which are able to sell a large part of their product within approximately 200 miles of their plants. In other words, the steel-making operation at Sydney was not in a very competitive position except in so far as rails and ingots and billets were concerned. In so far as its other products were concerned, it was likely to be what they call a residual producer for the rest of Canada. When the company exported to other countries it would find itself competing, not with the domestic steel-makers of those countries, but rather with other countries in which production costs were relatively low.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that the report comes to the conclusion that steelmaking in Sydney would go on based chiefly on production of rails, ingots and billets for use by Dosco and possibly by Siderurgie de Quebec at their flat rolling mills in the St. Lawrence valley, in addition, of course, to supplying the relatively small market in the Atlantic provinces.
Evidently, Mr. Speaker, since the time Dosco participated in the preparation of this report they have come to the conclusion that this basic operation is beyond their capacity, that even these limited objects are beyond the capacity of the owners of Dosco. When I say they have come to the conclusion that these objects are beyond their capacity, what I mean is that they have come to the conclusion it is not profitable for them to continue .production at Sydney, that they can take their capital and their managerial skills and employ them more profitably elsewhere. But this does not necessarily mean that they cannot make money at Sydney.
There are certain questions, Mr. Speaker, that I think we all ought to consider seriously when we look at the problem created by the announcement of Dosco. First, there is the intimation by Dosco that they will incur losses. In this connection I think that a meeting between company officials and provincial and federal government representatives would be most useful.
I should like to refer to the press release put out last Friday by Dosco. On page 2 of the press release appears the following:
Mr. Eramert's statement continued, "We are keenly aware of the impact our decision will have on the mill's employees, the Sydney community and the province of Nova Scotia and deeply regret that no other course is available within the corporation's abilities. Neither Dosco, nor Hawker Sid-
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant
deley (Canada) Ltd., which owns 77 per cent of the corporation, can continue to obsorb losses of the magnitude now being incurred." Dosco has reported losses, before income tax adjustments, of $4.3 million in 1986 and $6.4 million in the first six months of 1967.
Does that mean, Mr. Speaker, as one might think on superficial consideration, that Dosco is losing all this money in steel-making at Sydney and on the crude steel from Sydney that is used at Contrecoeur? Does it mean that the whole Dosco enterprise is losing a considerable sum of money? Are we being told that the Dosco operation generally is inefficient, and that because of this general inefficiency the company is now unable to continue at what it may regard as its least profitable base, namely Sydney? These questions have to be answered because they bear directly upon what ought to be done by the province of Nova Scotia, and anyone who wishes to be associated with the province of Nova Scotia in this, in facing up to the social problem created by the Dosco announcement.
I think that if the representatives of Dosco and Hawker Siddeley (Canada) Ltd. are not prepared to come to a public meeting and explain frankly what they mean-to put the residual heirs, if I may use that word in this context, into the economic picture in regard to their Sydney operation-it would be quite within the rules of propriety for the assembly in Halifax to summon before it the representatives of the corporation to explain precisely what these statements that have been put out mean.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan). I think there will have to be a public examination of at least the basic facts. It may be necessary also to ask the company to give information privately that would be helpful to those who are going to take up the problem from which Dosco appears determined to flee.
That is one question, Mr. Speaker, and a second question concerns the continued operation of the plant. I think it would be ridiculous to suggest that this operation can be closed out in six or seven months. This is an utterly ludicrous proposal. I am sure that everyone who has any obligation in this matter will see to it that the communities concerned simply do not have to deal with the kind of dislocations that would inevitably be entailed within this short period of time. It is utterly unthinkable that almost the entire industrial base of a city of considerable size should be closed down almost as if it had been hit by enemy attack.
3142	COMMONS
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant
I am not in a position, because I do not have the economic tacts, to say whether or not this plant ought to be continued in operation over many years, but I think it is appropriate for the layman to say that it is ridiculous to suggest that within half a year, and starting immediately, you can cut off the economic foundations of an entire community. The plant simply has to stay open; it is as plain and obvious, I think, as that.
Connected with the question whether or not the plant should stay open is a third question. I think that the speeches which have been made here this afternoon reveal that there is very little confidence among the members of this house, at least among those who have spoken, in Dosco. The arrangements for the future ownership and management of the plant are not a question that I think I ought to prejudge. That is largely a question to be answered by the members of the Nova Scotia assembly.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It is now clear that the financial assistance that may be necessary to keep the plant open ought not to be placed largely under the unguided control of Dosco. I do not want to prejudge the question of provincial nationalization of the company, but it well may be that the assembly can find that it has no real alternative. Nationalization would create great problems-let there be no doubt about that-particularly when one came to market the product, unless one could make an agreement with Dosco to use the Sydney production at its Contrecoeur flat rolling mills. Yet the problem of the Sydney community simply cannot be pushed aside because of the difficulties that would attend provincial nationalization.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria referred to the matter of transportation. The report on Sydney steel-making makes one realize that in the view of those who wrote the report the costs of transportation are most important. I am not at all satisfied that we ought not to take a much closer look at this aspect of the problem to see if something can be done in this area to render more viable the operation at Sydney.
Another point that ought to be emphasized is the question of pushing ahead as rapidly as possible at the Strait of Canso. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources referred to this development as one of the new foundations for the society of modern Nova Scotia. I think he is correct. But you know, Mr. 
DEBATES	October 16, 1967
Speaker, there is a remarkable contrast between the way a private company can close down a business and the way government departments go about opening up an area. Private companies seem to snap their fingers, make their decisions and close plants within weeks. It seems to take months or years to get anything as attractive as the economic development of the Strait of Canso area well under way. There should be, I think, a good deal of co-operation between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Nova Scotia in the Strait area immediately, particularly if it is clear that in the long run the steel-making operation cannot be continued.
I wish to put one final point before the house, Mr. Speaker. When I spoke in the house on October 3, 1967, about the housing question I said that there comes a point at which the savings made by concentrating industry are outbalanced by the costs of concentration. That point, I think, ought to be borne in mind by governments as they look at the questions posed by the Dosco announcement concerning steel-making at its Sydney plant. It is easy to say, "All right, Dosco has made its decision. It has decided that for it this is not the most profitable way to invest its resources. That is the economic decision and that is the decision that should prevail." But, I ask you, sir, how many indirect subsidies will go to steel-making elsewhere, whether at the managerial or employee level? In the long run, what is the most economical approach for the Canadian taxpayer? Which bill will be bigger for the Canadian taxpayer? Meeting the costs of making life tolerable in great metropolitan conglomerations or making it possible for steel-making to continue in Sydney, thereby making possible the continuation of that city?
I do not think the answer to that question is obvious at all. Those who rely simply on allegedly economic arguments when dealing with such questions often deceive themselves and thereby penalize the Canadian taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members who have spoken today I welcome your decision to grant an adjournment debate on the important question placed before you in the motion presented by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis). As Your Honour indicated this afternoon, I too sent you a notice of motion on the same subject, so
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant that had the hon. member for Cape Breton South not moved his, you would have had a motion before you in terms which I might be permitted to place on the record, namely, that there be an adjournment of the house under standing order 26-
-for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the recent announcement that the steel plant of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation at Sydney, Nova Scotia, is to be closed in 1968, and the need for an immediate statement by the government as to the steps it will take to make sure that this mortal blow to the people and the economy of Cape Breton Island does not take place.
I thought I would like to read that motion, not only to place on the record the terms in which we would have presented it, but to emphasize the fact that we feel, as I now sense all members of the house do, that this would be a mortal blow to the people of eastern Nova Scotia, if the basic steel industry were shut down on Cape Breton Island. We feel it is not only important that parliament be allowed to discuss this matter today, but even more important that the government take action, and take action soon.
I must say that I was quite disappointed in the approach to this problem taken this afternoon by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin), but before I comment on what he said today I should like to draw attention to something else that I think calls for an explanation. He told us or shall I say he confirmed in the house this afternoon what we read in the press over the week end, namely that the Hawker Siddeley people met with certain members of the government, including himself, last Thursday to inform them of the intended action of Dosco at Sydney. It was made quite clear this afternoon that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources knew on Thursday last that the steel mill at Sydney was to be closed in April, 1968. Yet on Friday last, as recorded in Hansard at page 3064, the hon. member for Cape Breton South put this question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources:
Could the minister indicate when he expects that the board of the Cape Breton Development Corporation will be appointed, and when they will begin their work?
Let me now read the answer and the rest of the exchange.

I find it hard to understand that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources could know on Thursday that the Dosco steel mill was to be closed in April next, yet on Friday could say to this house that he knew of nothing that was going to worsen the problem faced by the Cape Breton Development Corporation. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that he knew not only something had taken place which would worsen the problem but he knew of something which would make it practically impossible for the corporation to function at all, under the terms of the legislation given to it by the parliament of Canada.
However, Mr. Speaker, the main response of the minister this afternoon, apart from his interesting account of things that have been done in recent years in the Cape Breton area, was to write off quickly the only positive suggestion made, namely the suggestion of my colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) which was a repetition of the proposal we made last June and earlier, that the entire Dosco operation should be nationalized. The minister was ready with a quick answer. He said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North was ready with an answer-instant nationalization; and the minister's comment was supposed to get rid of the hon. member's suggestion.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the saddest thing that took place this afternoon was the way in which the minister made an instant rejection of the only positive suggestion that has been made for coping with this problem. He stood in his place and told us that there are certain difficulties in connection with nationalization. Of course there are. The difficulties he recited, however, were mainly with regard to the question concerning what would happen if the government were to nationalize part of an industry; that is, where would it stand with regard to the other part of that industry or with regard to other industries in Canada?
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Does the minister not know that in Canada today we own publicly the Canadian National Railways but that we do not own all

the railways in Canada? Does he not know that we own publicly Air Canada but that we do not have a complete monopoly over the air industry in this country? Does he not know that we the people of Canada own the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation but that we do not own C.T.V.? Does he not know that we own publicly the Polymer Corporation but that that has not put the other rubber companies out of business? Does he not know that we the people of Canada own the government printing bureau which turns out some of the finest printing done in North America but that this has not put the other printing companies in Canada out of business? Does he not know that the telephone industry in this country is partly publicly and partly privately owned?
I suggest it was sheer nonsense for the minister to negate the suggestion that we could nationalize part of an industry. The government of Canada and the governments of the various provinces are engaged in all kinds of businesses and services. Surely the minister, from his academic experience if from no other, knows that around the world where developing countries are trying to cope with their problems, particularly in areas where things are difficult economically, public ownership, nationalization and socialization are the answers people have to resort to. I believe that rather than cavalierly dismiss the suggestion from this corner as being instant nationalization and something which could not be considered, the government ought to take it into consideration.
I thought the hon. member for Antigo-nish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) was a little embarrassed by the quick and ready way in which his ministerial colleague dismissed nationalization. Therefore he filled in a bit by suggesting that maybe provincial nationalization might be considered. Does he not realize, when we are talking about nationalization at this point, that the Cape Breton Development Corporation has been set up and that it is a federally incorporated crown company which already has been given power by parliament to nationalize and take over the coal operation? Does it not seem the part of logic and common sense that if we are to have nationalization in the same area, in another operation of the same company, that it would be far better for it to be nationalization at the federal rather than at the provincial level? However, I do not wish to be too hard on my friend from Antigonish-Guysborough, because he at least made up for the way in which the

Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources dismissed the whole question of nationalization.
Does the hon. member wish to ask a question?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the two questions. The hon. member seems to think that public ownership thus far is only in the field of utilities and never in the field of services or materials. I suggest that the Polymer Corporation which is in the business of producing rubber, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the printing bureau are providing not just services but actual goods. I suggest there are many examples of public ownership in fields other than so-called utilities such as light, power and so on. As a matter of fact I think it is a pretxy thin line to draw, so far as the railways are concerned, as to whether this is purely a utility or a service.
The other question the hon. member asked me is one I particularly welcome. He wishes to know whether I should not distinguish between the coal operation and the steel operation in Cape Breton Island. The main point I wish to make, and the main point we in this group have been trying to make for a long period, is that one must look at the problem in Cape Breton Island in its entirety. To put it in the simplest and most understandable terms, I think there should be a T.V.A. type project instituted in Cape Breton Island. We think it is tragic and indeed a crime that there are still in Canada as many depressed areas as there are. I believe it would be a crime if we were to sit idly by and let another such area develop in Cape Breton Island. If the government were to step in with a T.V.A. type plan, the whole of Cape Breton Island could be made a model community. We
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant think the government should try to do a full dress job in Cape Breton Island.

It was precisely because this was made clear to us, and that this legislation was then concerned about coal but apparently not about steel, that we in this party made the speeches we made at that time and moved an amendment to enlarge that bill. Some very significant if not prophetic words were uttered by the leader of this party, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), on June 15 as recorded at page 1582 of Hansard. Let me quote some of his words:
The minister said a few moments ago that to include the steel industry in this development corporation would not gain widespread support. I do not know on what the minister bases that statement. If there is one thing the government ought to learn, it is that the art of governing is the art of foreseeing. It is not a matter of waiting until the government is pressed into doing something. It is a matter of the government seeing the signs that are all about it that the steel industry in Cape Breton island is in trouble. The government should not wait until the steel mill is closed, but should do something about it now.
That was our plea in June, a plea we made not only in speeches by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), but one that we put to the house in the form of an amendment moved by the hon. member for York South to clause 23 in an endeavour to get the rights of the corporation enlarged so it could go into the other industry rather than just coal, namely steel.
When that amendment was moved on June 27, as recorded at page 2308 of Hansard, the Minister of National Health and Welfare immediately rose on a point of order. I have reread his statement on the point of order and there is no doubt that it was a point of order speech. However it also reflected his belief that this was the kind of thing that should not be done, that steel should not at this point be brought under the aegis of the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
After a procedural debate which took up five or six pages in Hansard the chairman of the committee of the whole rules that the amendment was in order and a vote was taken. This was one of those votes that do not require ringing of the bells, so only those

It can be said, and I know it will be said, that in the house today on this issue all of us have reflected our points of view. The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) spoke mainly about what the Bank of Canada might do. The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston) put in his pitch that this debate should not be used to pillory private enterprise. However, on this particular issue it has become clear that unless we do go in for an extensive practice of public ownership or national ownership for Cape Breton Island, the island is going to become not the place of natural beauty it has been but a depressed area so far as the people who live there are concerned.
I was also concerned and disappointed with the statement made today by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand). He started out fine, and I thought our friend had turned into a trade unionist again, when he referred to social responsibility on the part of big corporations, and when he told us how immoral it was for big corporations not to take into consideration the rights of those people who work for them. That part of his speech was excellent and deserved the applause it received. But I could not help wondering what the government of which he is a member has done about the Freedman report which deals with this matter. The government has had that report for some time.
After the minister had completed this nice little lecture, with which we all agreed, he had a little salve for certain wounds, and was happy to announce that his department would do its best to come forward with alternative arrangements for those who would be put out of work. The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria then asked whether there was to be a revival of the recommendation of

the Gordon report that these people be assisted to move out of Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) again attempted to correct the mistake of his minister by saying that he felt there were arguments for doing something else than concentrating people in a few big cities. There is a great deal being said these days about national unity. I do not intend to move into a discussion of the aspect of that problem which is uppermost in our minds these days, but surely one of the things we must accomplish if we are really going to have national unity is equal economic conditions and equal economic opportunities across this country. It is not good enough to give short notice to the workers of Air Canada at Winnipeg that they are going to be out of jobs, and not good enough to give even shorter notice to this larger number of workers in Cape Breton that their jobs are disappearing, and that they will have no opportunity to maintain any kind of decent life in that beautiful Cape Breton Island.
Let me say again that we are all obliged to you, Mr. Speaker, for your decision to permit a discussion of this matter today on the motion moved by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis). As one with ancestral roots in Nova Scotia I know something of the untoward economic conditions of that province and what they have done to people in the past. I do not think these things should be repeated. Indeed, we should go further than just stemming the tide of difficulties there. We should seize this opportunity to make the social and economic life of Cape Breton Island that of a model community. This could be done if we just stop worrying about cliches and doctrinaire positions. I hope the seriousness of this crisis will challenge the government of this country to deal with it as it ought to be dealt with, for the sake of the people of Cape Breton Island and for the sake of the good name of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, let me join with previous speakers during the discussion this afternoon and evening in expressing appreciation to yourself and to hon. members on the benches opposite for allowing the opportunity to discuss at least among ourselves the very serious situation which has now developed in Cape Breton and indeed in the province of Nova Scotia. This is not a problem that finds its beginning and end in the city of Sydney and its immediate environs and neighbouring areas. This difficulty is shared by those on the mainland, in the

[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Many observations made this afternoon are very pertinent. I hope that many of the suggestions will be helpful to the minister from Nova Scotia in his discussions next week with representatives of community and industry in their searching, through discussion, to arrive at a resolution of this problem. It is indeed a very serious problem. I believe we all realize this, and that a solution must soon be found. We have had today an opportunity to consider the seriousness of the problem. We have had an opportunity to consider some of the suggestions that have been made. It has been suggested that nationalization is a solution to the problem. The question is, federally or provincially, who can afford to do this?
In the final analysis, having made the decision in this respect, will it guarantee economic feasibility? The industry must find markets for its products. I believe this is a very pertinent question to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and his colleagues must address themselves next week. Hawker Siddeley, in the field of primary production and manufacturing, is the 31st largest corporate entity in the world, outside the United States of America. The sales of this company were last year in excess of $1 billion. These sales were directly attributable to production. We are not dealing with a small, corporate entity. This is one of the largest companies operating in Europe today. If it is to maintain its growth and development, it must continue to be very ruthless. We are not dealing with a company that is flush with funds and can easily raise new capital. Indeed, we must bear in mind the words of Sir Roy Dobson in this context, that as far as the interests of this corporation in Canada are concerned, the company has to be self capitalizing.
It does not take too much depth of knowledge to look at the financial situation of such companies in Canada and their position and be at once a little alarmed. I suggest to the minister from Nova Scotia that his duties are now indeed very serious. This minister now has an opportunity, as he has not had for many years, to show that the present government is capable of responsible leadership. The government can show this leadership in the manner in which they approach the problem.
October 16, 1967

Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant They can show leadership by the degree to which they keep in the forefront of their minds the very serious situation which would exist in Trenton and the city of Halifax if Dosco continues to find it too difficult to operate in Sydney.
Myself, the citizens of Nova Scotia, the premier of that province, and Dr. MacKeough, who is the chairman of the special committee studying this subject, would be very pleased if the government would clarify the many questions which are in the minds of all people in the Atlantic community. These questions resolve themselves into whether or not there is a viable market for the production of the plant. If necessary, government at one level or another should take steps to see that the industry continues. This can only be done if it is shown that there is a market for the production of this plant.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If this cannot be done, heaven only knows what the answer is. I do not pretend to know. But I do know that if this attitude, which already has been called deplorable-and indeed is-is allowed to continue and go outside the present context so as to embrace the Trenton plant, the Halifax shipyards and the Dartmouth marine slip, it will be a blow to Halifax from which I doubt it will be able to recover in the immediate future.
The port of Halifax is handicapped by an indecisive attitude on the part of this government, which has a fear of or inability to define its policy. This is perhaps the best opportunity of hon. members from Nova Scotia to show concern for the problem and leadership in its solution. Halifax has seen a very serious decline of port activity. We have suffered the very recent deleterious impact of the so-called l.c.l. freight rates. These are just two of the serious problems that affect my area.
These problems are related to the decision of Hawker Siddeley to cease its operations in six months time. The over-all impact of this decision has already been placed clearly on the record. Hon. members have referred to the number of people who will be directly or indirectly adversely involved. People are people. They are human beings entitled to some respect for their human dignity and individuality. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) this afternoon spoke in glowing terms of a concern for a situation which appears to be developing in Canada. It is the tendency of large corporate
(Mr. Forrestall.l
entities in this country to make decisions such as this. The minister referred to the Bell Island situation and what is taking place in regard to manpower.
Nobody of course disagrees with what the minister said. He did seem to show a little more concern than has been evidenced by the actions of Dosco or its parent company Hawker Siddeley. This is fine. However, it pays only lip service to a situation we would all like to see exist but which in fact does not exist. The fact is that a different situation exists.
I would caution the minister during his deliberations and talks in the next few days that he should not approach the resolution of the problem at the expense of any other viable economic activity in the Atlantic provinces, but that he should find an answer which works for the betterment of all Nova Scotians, and not simply the resolution of the problem that is facing the people on Cape Breton right now. I am sure the minister will do this, and so will those who will be his colleagues in the resolution of the problem and on whose shoulders a very basic responsibility lies, namely the officials in the provincial government of Nova Scotia. I am sure that together they will find an answer to this problem.
I wish now to go back very briefly to the events of the last week end. At a meeting of mayors and other civic leaders in the Atlantic area held in Moncton at the invitation of Mayor Jones it was said that the whole matter of economic activity in the Atlantic provinces is in serious need of responsible leadership. We have had shotgun approaches to all of our problems in the last five or six years. There has been a great lack of intelligent and meaningful study of what our problems are and how they can be overcome.
The recommendations of the second, third and indeed what appears to be the fourth annual report . of the Economic Council of Canada continue to be largely ignored,-so much so in fact that the mayors of our various cities directly involved in the economy of the Atlantic area, in a communique issued over the week end, have seen fit to criticize severely the present government for its lack of effective action in areas such as transportation, port development, and the inter and in-tra regional movement of freight. Perhaps it goes without saying that we in Ottawa must come to some early conclusion-as to just what it is that we intend to do about regional disparity.
October 16, 1967

We have gone on for many years hoping that time will resolve the problems of the Atlantic area, but there has been no evidence in the last two or three years that we are any closer to even describing the types of problems that are facing us. We are just now seeing the manifestations of one of the great ones in the decision taken by Dosco to close its operation. We must very shortly move to much more meaningful long term answers. If we do not, then I am afraid that the next 100 years will be no better for the Atlantic provinces than the first 100 years.
If the governement opposite has any doubts as to the seriousness of this, I would ask them simply to read tomorrow the words of the hon. members for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir). What they and other speakers had to say today with regard to the economic and social situation which will be brought about if this plant is not sustained are thoughts that came straight from their hearts, and that were born out of an experience and an awareness of the role which the steel community has played in Sydney. On my part they are voiced because I am aware of the role which Dosco plays in the port of Halifax. I am aware of the fact that if Dosco can so easily withdraw from Sydney it could very easily withdraw from the port of Halifax the only major ship repair facility that we have.
The other indicators of lack of government planning were dealt with very extensively last spring. These involve the attitudes of the government with regard to defence spending. In one sense the attitude of Hawker Siddeley and Dosco toward Sydney is no different from the attitude that is creeping in with regard to our armed forces and our national defence posture. I am not saying whether or not the government is right in its national defence posture. What I am saying is that this need-to-know philosophy, this built-in fear of telling people what must be done, must come to an end. People cannot operate in a vacuum. Industry cannot plan and the supporting services cannot orient themselves if they do not know what is to happen. The best agency to tell them is the government, and it must accept this responsibility. I do not charge the government with anything in particular right now because I think the news has been to them as much of a surprise as it has to everyone else. But I do say to them that if they are to be charged with anything they should be charged with not having known that this was to take place. There were many

Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant indicators. The government has been questioned in this house for the last 18 months by the Cape Breton members, but when the news came it came as a great shock. I think the government was remiss in that respect.
So as not to take up any more time of the house, Mr. Speaker, let me close by making one observation, namely that if closure of the mine does in fact take place, it must largely be the consequence of the federal economic, tariff, transportation, and freight rate policies, and other activities.
I suspect that right now there is very little that the province of Nova Scotia can do to overcome the economic problem that has been created, except to provide leadership. I do not know what role it can play in terms of dollars and cents but I do know it will have to be limited. Unless the matter is properly resolved, perhaps in the final analysis we must ask the following question, as did the Chronicle-Herald of today's date in the lead editorial:
The question that Nova Scotians must ask themselves, and the federal government also, is, are we Canadians deserving of the same treatment as other regions of this great and wealthy country?
I suggest that the onus of answering that question to the satisfaction not only of the people in Sydney but of the entire Atlantic community lies largely in the hands of the committee of the cabinet which has been established to look into this problem, in the degree to which it will co-operate with the corresponding group set up by Hon. speechtext:
It is not my intention to speak at great length
on the motion presently before the house; but, speaking as a Nova Scotian and a Canadian, I wish to endorse the remarks of my colleagues with regard to the serious economic stituation faced by many Nova Scotians as a result of the announcement by the management of Dosco that they will cease production on April 30, 1968. This announcement shocked and numbed all Nova Scotians; its effect has spread like an earthquake across the industrial part of Canada. This in
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant fact is not a provincial problem; it is a national problem.
For more than 60 years coal and steel have been the twin economic backbones of industrial Cape Breton, an area peopled by hardy descendants and settlers from Ireland and Scotland. The steel mill was built in the year 1900. If Dosco succeeds in abandoning the mill, which is the smallest of our four basic steel plants and if the coal mines are closed on schedule, the entire way of life in Cape Breton, in our province-in fact, throughout Canada-will be drastically altered within the next 18 months.
Ever since the closing announcement, interested Canadians have all been asking the same question: What will happen to the more than 2,600 steel men who will be thrown out of work next April? Unemployment is already quite high in this part of Nova Scotia; only a year ago approximately 3,700 men were employed when two blast furnaces were in operation. Now only one is in operation. With the phasing out of the coal mining operation a feeling of gloom pervades the entire area. The steel men I have mentioned are directly affected; yet, literally thousands of others will be indirectly affected when and if Dosco should carry out its plan.
The manner of the announcement caused consternation to government leaders at federal and provincial levels. According to reports, Premier G.I. Smith of Nova Scotia has said that Dosco lacked a sense of corporate responsibility to its employees and the community; the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) is reported to be deeply shocked, as well he might be.
The question arises: Can we as a nation afford to let an industry of such great importance to Nova Scotia and Canada die of economic strangulation? I do not believe we can. I believe it is the responsibility of the federal and provincial authorities to put their heads together in the hope of finding a solution to the problem.
I should like to know what has happened to the Hawker Siddeley management within the past month; is that industry drastically affected by changes in the Kennedy round talks at Geneva? Have they been reading the Financial Post of October 7 which shows how the inflation virus spreads. Sixteen causes are listed and I think I ought to read some of them into the record. Here is one:
The persistent rise in living costs has left the Canadian dollar of 1925 worth barely 50c today. The current erosion in Canada and the U.S. is the fastest since Korea.
October 16, 1967

Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant
Here is another:
Sales taxes have inflated the cost of building materials and construction wage rates are up sharply. But reflecting urban population pressures, the fastest rise is in land prices.
Here is yet another:
The heaviest pressure now on consumer prices comes from services-largely because labor costs are rising and services depend on substantial quantities of labor.
And here is another
But manufacturing wage rates in both Canada and the U.S. are now rising more rapidly than a few years ago. And the advance in Canada is currently twice as fast as it is in the U.S.
Here is another:
Higher wage rates are putting large new pressures on industry selling prices because they are coming at a point when productivity gains are considerably smaller than they were.
And here is another:
With more industries hiking prices, the main index of wholesale prices is rising. The specially steep climb in Canada suggests a less competitive position for Canadian-made goods.
Is this the reason for the company's action? Here is yet another:
Canada's money supply is being expanded at a rapid clip to help finance heavy government borrowing and to prod the economy into creating new jobs for a fast-growing work force.
I say to the government that it is high time they stopped thinking of ways of spending money without getting any return; it is high time they thought of getting some value for the money we have. That is what we need, some purchasing power in our dollar, instead of the excessive spending that everybody is worried about and the extravagance and waste indulged in by this government.
Finally I shall read this from the same copy of the Financial Post:
The impact of fast-escalating spending by all governments in Canada is inflating demand for money, goods, services and will continue to do so until spending programs are cut back.
Did the management read these items? Is what I have read that which influenced them to reach their decision? Did they realize that their future under this administration is not as good as it might be? I should like to know what happened.
Their action in announcing the closing of the steel mill is a complete reversal of the statement made earlier in co-operation with the Nova Scotia Voluntary Economic Planning Board and the Atlantic Development Board. At that time they were in complete agreement with the release of a report which

stated that the future of the Sydney mills as a supplier of ingots and rails was assured, under existing conditions.
I must submit that the report does not paint a rosy future for the Cape Breton steel men; nevertheless, it should be of considerable assistance to the Cape Breton Development Corporation in determining the priorities for the economic development of the Cape Breton area.
In a speech this afternoon the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) put on record some of the conclusions of the voluntary planning board of the province of Nova Scotia. At the risk of repeating what he said I wish to read some of the conclusions of that body. They are as follows:
Sydney does not possess actual or potential production cost advantages in relation to other actual or potential competitive sites in Canada or abroad.
Successful steelmaking throughout the world today depends upon a mill having a local or natural market area of sufficient size to absorb fixed costs, i.e., that portion of costs which does not vary with production volume.
o (9:20 p.m.)
Sydney's natural market is the Atlantic region, and the region's steel consumption is much too small to absorb Sydney's fixed costs. About 85 per cent of Sydney's production must be sold in areas beyond the Atlantic region. The attendant freight costs place Sydney in a position of disadvantage vis-a-vis other factors.
Import competition is severe in most product lines in the eastern part of Canada where Dosco seeks its major sales volume.
In finished rolled-steel products (excluding rails) Sydney is in the position of a residual supplier to Canadian customers beyond the Atlantic region.
In export markets, including the U.S. and Britain, Sydney is in competition with third country exporters rather than with the local producers.
World export prices are depressed to levels which generally do not cover the fixed and variable production costs of exporters.
Export sales in new product lines could be generated, but not in sufficient volume at prices adequate to justify the installation of new facilities at Sydney.
There is a statement that bears thorough study. Who knows what volume could be accomplished in the next year or two?
The future role of Sydney is expected to be primarily that of a supplier of ingots and billets to Quebec mills for rolling and as a manufacturer of rails.
The establishment of Dosco's rolling mills at
Contrecoeur provides Sydney with its best assurance of continued operation, and prospects for some expansion of primary-steel production.
The prospects for rapidly expanding steel demand in the Atlantic region to provide Sydney with a sounder economic base can be regarded with only limited optimism.
October 16, 1967

Because the present plans of Sidbec (the Quebec government-sponsored steel project) are unknown, the implications for Sydney of a Sidbec plant are entirely a matter of speculation. Some form of co-operation between Dosco and Sidbec cannot be ruled out, and might be beneficial to both companies and both provinces.
This is the report of the Nova Scotia Voluntary Economic Planning Board, and it is the report that was agreed to by Dosco. Is it any wonder that Dosco's announcement has virtually shocked everyone in Nova Scotia and throughout Canada?
Mr. Emmert, chairman and president of Dosco, said his decision to close the plant was forced because of non-competitive production costs at Sydney, together with shipping costs between the mill and major market areas in Canada. He said the company has become increasingly aware that its Sydney works has an abnormally high cost of production due to its age and attendant maintenance and manning costs. He also said steel capacity throughout the world has eroded prices in the already depressed market served by Dosco steel, and this factor in turn has prevented wage increases from being sufficiently recovered through increased production or selling prices.
Now, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Emmert is not alone in facing this problem of rising costs and heavy competition. The United States has a similar problem, and it is interesting to note the action that has been proposed in that country to support its steel industry. According to the Financial Times of Canada of October 16, today's date, the United States steel lobby has succeeded in convincing a large group of usually free trade minded senators to sponsor and support new legislation aimed at retaliating against foreign countries which discriminate against United States steel exports. The proposed bill would give the President of the United States 180 days in which to negotiate bilateral or multilateral international agreements under which other countries would voluntarily restrict their steel exports to the United States to levels no higher than their average share of the United States market during the 1964-66 period. In effect the bill would freeze total United States steel imports at about 9.5 per cent of total American steel consumption. The reason for this action is set out in the Financial Times as follows:
The United States steel industry contends that non-tariff discrimination is the basis for the domestic industry's inability to compete in foreign markets. A flat 6 per cent to 7 per cent duty is imposed on all steel imports into the United States. The duty is levied on the wholesale value of the
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant steel at the point of shipment and is not levied on the freight and insurance costs, which can add as much as 13 per cent to the value of the landed steel.
By comparison, Belgium levies, over and above its normal duties, a tax ranging from 7 per cent to 19 per cent on the duty-paid value of imported steel. France imposes a 25 per cent sales tax and a 0.2 per cent custom stamp tax over and above normal duties. West Germany imposes a turnover equalization tax of 7.5 per cent to 9.5 per cent and Italy imposes a 4 per cent sales tax and a compensatory import tax of 4.8 per cent to 6.5 per cent.
Japan, 40 per cent of whose exports go to the United States, has a system of import licences and currency controls that virtually excludes United States steel from its markets.
The bill to be introduced this week is aimed at retaliating against countries that have imposed such barriers.
Here is an interesting point.
Canadian steel shipments to the United States last year totalled $104 million, or less than 10 per cent of total United States steel imports.'At the same time, United States steel exports to Canada totalled $196 million, or more than one third of total United States steel exports.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, we bought some $92 million more worth of steel from the United States than we were able to sell to that country.
In my opinion, this action that has been taken by Dosco will make Sydney a disaster area. Disaster conditions require drastic action. Nova Scotians were told when the St. Lawrence seaway was built that it would be helpful to their economy. We heard speakers from the Liberal party, now in power, who travelled through Atlantic Canada and made this claim. I am not being critical of them for making those statements at that time, but I ask the government to re-examine its proposals of that date.
In his brief speech a few moments ago the hon. member for Medicine .Hat (Mr. Olson) asked us for suggestions. I say to the government, re-examine your proposals made at the time when you proposed the establishment of the seaway; see if there is something you overlooked to lower our costs for waterborne steel to the central markets of Canada. This was one of the items stressed by the voluntary planning board, and again I quote it:
Import competition is severe in most product lines in the eastern part of Canada where Dosco seeks its major sales volume.
I have no doubt that this is true. If this is
so, then it is the responsibility of government to see if we cannot use this waterway from the Atlantic provinces to central markets to lower costs and keep the mill open in the city of Sydney.
October 16, 1967

Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant
1 would also urge the government to examine the possible application o 1 tariffs to protect our steel industry, as other countries are doing or, alternatively, to discuss with other countries the elimination of their tariffs. Surely a small country like Canada with 20 million people should have its steel exports in balance with the United States.
If no agreement on tariffs can be reached we may well be required to give consideration to legislation similar to that which is being proposed in the United States. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because we hear a lot today about social security in Canada. I am in favour of social security, but in my opinion the best social security we can give any man is the assurance of a good job with a good future. This is what we want in Canada today. This is the kind of social security we need.
The step that was proposed last week in Sydney can hardly be justified no matter how we look at it, but anything we can do at the federal level to help alleviate the misery and suffering can be justified. There will be misery and suffering in Cape Breton if the mill closes next April. This is a matter that cannot be passed over lightly. It is a problem that should receive the immediate attention of the best brains in our federal and provincial governments if our dream of a developing Canada, as publicized during our centennial celebrations, is not to die with the closing of Expo.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest and more than ordinary concern to the debate that was precipitated this afternoon by the motion of the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis). I appreciate the motivation behind the motion. I believe the seriousness of the situation has been supported by the unanimity with which the house agreed to this emergency debate.
I rise with a heavy heart really to participate in this debate in this closing moment, because I realize, as do other hon. members, the impact that this decision if implemented will have on the immediate employees at the steel plant at Sydney, and also upon the general economy of Nova Scotia as a whole. The impact of this decision if implemented will be very great and very brutal. Unless the impact can be averted or unless some solutions are found to cushion its effect, in my judgment the sudden discharge of 3,000 men onto the

labour market in Cape Breton at the end of April or May would lead to a near collapse of the industrial economy of that area.
When we set up the Cape Breton Development Corporation we were aware that the closure of the Cape Breton coal mines and the sudden cessation of mining operations would not be bearable by the economy. We realized that if these collieries closed suddenly and
6,000	or 7,000 men were discharged into the labour market there would be no real foundation for the economic existence of that area. While the numbers involved in this particular field are not as great as the coal industry, the impact upon the economy will be very great, very sharp and very unfortunate.
This debate has produced no immediate solution to the problem, because I think most of us are still somewhat bewildered by the suddenness of the decision and still somewhat incapable of relating the decision to recent events and recent impressions we have received. For example, it was only in the spring of this year that an agreement involving the provincial government, the federal govern-nent and Dosco was reached to provide for almost $6 million in Sydney for the provision of docking facilities or bulk handling facilities. There was an understanding in the agreement that this amount of money which was being made available by federal and provincial funds would be matched by an equivalent investment in the industry by the corporation over a period of time. Certainly one had some indication that an agreement of that kind was not to be the messenger of an immediate decision to close out an industry or a plant.

speechtext:
Yes, the agreement is explicit on that point. If there should be any doubt as to the carrying out of this undertaking, there is a provision in the agreement that the arbitration will be conducted by the chief justice of the province of Nova Scotia. Just recently, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) and others, a steel making study was produced under the joint auspices of the Atlantic Development Board, the Nova Scotia Voluntary Planning Council, which is an agency of the provincial government, and the Dosco corporation. Since I have taken on
October 16, 1967

the responsibility for the Atlantic Development Board I have given my consent to the release of that study. It was concurred in, not two years ago, or a year ago, or a few months ago, but quite recently, by the highest officers in the Dosco corporation. While none of us would argue that this steel making study gave any strong basis for optimism or a strong basis to believe that the steel industry in Sydney would be a growing industry or an increasing user of labour, or indeed that it did not have very important difficulties, nevertheless one of the conclusions on the positive side was that for an indefinite period at least this plant could look forward to being the basic supplier of ingots and billets to the Quebec mills.
It is no wonder that most of us who were keeping abreast of developments were shocked and stunned at the decision that was conveyed to the government of Canada last Thursday morning by the chairman of Hawker Siddeley in Britain, the chairman in Canada and the president of Dosco. The reasons which have been given by the responsible officers may be very strong and convincing reasons to persons who are responsible for administering assets on behalf of shareholders, but it seems to me the method by which this decision was carried out is as brutal in a sense as the impact of the decision itself, because no effort was made to lay before the governments the problems which affected this industry, and there was no effort to explain to the employees and their families the difficulties involved in operating this plant. Who, after all, were more entitled to such explanations than these employees in a civilized community. No effort was made to consult with them or present to them any method or assistance by which what would be a calamity to the community could be averted.
I find even more objectionable the fact that the corporation up to the present time has refused, since it has taken this decision, to meet in an acceptable form the representatives of the two governments, the union leaders and the community leaders to explain the reasons for this decision or to outline, as I think they ought to, the method by which they intend to discharge their responsibilities relative to the work force and to the community.
Following the decision announced to us in Ottawa on Thursday we had a number of meetings and concluded that the most important first step would be to convene a meeting
Closing of Nova Scotia Steel Plant of this kind at Sydney at which the representatives of the corporation would explain their position. That is a very vital and important thing to have done, e (9:40 p.m.)
Acting on behalf of the government of Canada I sent a telegram to the premier of Nova Scotia suggesting such a meeting and, because the meeting would likely be held in Nova Scotia and because of the vital interest to that province, I suggested that he convene the meeting. The premier of Nova Scotia thought this was a reasonable request and concurred in it, but we propose to have a meeting tomorrow night in Sydney. However, so far as I know, there has been no indication yet that the representatives of this organization will be present. I understand that Sir Harold Hall, the chairman of the Hawker Siddeley group, flew to Britain shortly after the decision was announced. I am quite satisfied that this was not a Canadian decision, but that the decision was made in London and that the people of Nova Scotia have not had the opportunity of even hearing or seeing the person who is in a position to exercise such an economic force on their lives. It is my hope that the corporation in this period of great difficulty will at an early date attend discussions with all of us in respect of what can be done to avert this calamity.
The ideal solution is to find some way to keep this plant in operation, but that requires first of all, it seems to me, the co-operation of the corporations involved. Hon. members have suggested that the steel plant in Sydney become a public plant, and that it be operated by the federal government. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that when I present my reaction to this proposal, it is not based on any ideological or basic principle in opposition to the public authority undertaking something of this kind. However, bearing in mind that the Sydney steel plant is one part of a growing and competitive industry in Canada, it would present difficulties if a national government selected a single plant to be operated and supported with public funds in competition with other plants involved in the same industry in other parts of Canada.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-RESOLUTION FROM BRITISH COLUMBIA RESPECTING TOBACCO ADVERTISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a most unusual resolution adopted by the delegates at the union of British Columbia municipalities was brought to my attention. I think it is the first occasion that a convention of municipalities for any province has taken the time to deal with this subject and to have considerable debate on the resolution in question. I obtained a copy of the Trail Times of September 23, and I read from it as follows:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Municipal Delegates Veto All Cigarette Advertising.
Prince George (CP)-Municipal leaders called Friday for restrictions on tobacco advertising.
Delegates to the Union of B.C. Municipalities convention overruled their resolutions committee which said the Port Alberni proposal was not a matter for local governments.
"We must be a responsible body," said Dr. R. M. Heffelfinger, a Port Alberni alderman. "It is a matter for our concern and we should endorse the resolution." Mayor Les Hammer of Port Alberni argued that it is a municipal matter because medical evidence stressed the health hazard of smoking.
The city's resolution said:
"It is morally and ethically wrong to deliberately advertise products which are of no benefit whatever and are actually very injurious to young people and society generally."
Seek Laws.
It proposed that the U.B.C.M. call on senior governments to introduce legislation to "eliminate, modify or deglamorize all forms of tobacco advertising."
This resolution was the cause of a very interesting debate and, as I said before, it was the first occasion at which a convention of municipalities in any province has dealt with this type of resolution. I think it is based on the fact that the delegates at the convention were aware of the circumstances that they were criticizing so far as the advertising is concerned. That is why they supported the resolution.
Since the convention there has been a quite general interest in this matter throughout British Columbia and in the riding which I have the honour to represent. The matter has been discussed by other groups and there is general support for the action taken by the union of British Columbia municipalities convention.
It was on that account that I rose on October 2 to ask the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, based

Has the minister received a copy of this resolution and, if so, can he inform the house of his response to same.
